**Bräcke Municipality** ([Swedish](./Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Bräcke kommun*) is a [municipality](./Municipalities_of_Sweden "Municipalities of Sweden") in [Jämtland County](./Jämtland_County "Jämtland County") in northern [Sweden](./Sweden "Sweden"). Its [seat](./Administrative_centre "Administrative centre") is located in [Bräcke](./Bräcke "Bräcke").

The present municipality was formed in 1974 when "old" Bräcke Municipality was amalgamated with Kälarne and Revsund. The three former municipalities had been created in 1952. The number of original entities (as of 1863) were six. Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.

**Bräcke Municipality** ([Swedish](./Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Bräcke kommun*) is a [municipality](./Municipalities_of_Sweden "Municipalities of Sweden") in [Jämtland County](./Jämtland_County "Jämtland County") in northern [Sweden](./Sweden "Sweden"). Its [seat](./Administrative_centre "Administrative centre") is located in [Bräcke](./Bräcke "Bräcke").

The present municipality was formed in 1974 when "old" Bräcke Municipality was amalgamated with Kälarne and Revsund. The three former municipalities had been created in 1952. The number of original entities (as of 1863) were six. Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.

Notable people
--------------

One of the most famous people coming from Bräcke Municipality is the former [middle distance](./Middle_distance_track_event "Middle distance track event") runner and [world record holder](./World_record "World record") [Gunder Hägg](./Gunder_Hägg "Gunder Hägg"), who was born in the village [Albacken](./Albacken?action=edit&redlink=1 "Albacken") outside of the town Bräcke.

**Bräcke Municipality** ([Swedish](./Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Bräcke kommun*) is a [municipality](./Municipalities_of_Sweden "Municipalities of Sweden") in [Jämtland County](./Jämtland_County "Jämtland County") in northern [Sweden](./Sweden "Sweden"). Its [seat](./Administrative_centre "Administrative centre") is located in [Bräcke](./Bräcke "Bräcke").

The present municipality was formed in 1974 when "old" Bräcke Municipality was amalgamated with Kälarne and Revsund. The three former municipalities had been created in 1952. The number of original entities (as of 1863) were six. Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.

------------

This is a demographic table based on Bräcke Municipality's electoral districts in the [2022 Swedish general election](./2022_Swedish_general_election "2022 Swedish general election") sourced from [SVT](./Swedish_Television "Swedish Television")'s election platform, in turn taken from [SCB](./Statistiska_Centralbyrån "Statistiska Centralbyrån") official statistics.[[4]](./Bräcke_Municipality#cite_note-BräckeVal2022-4)

--------------

One of the most famous people coming from Bräcke Municipality is the former [middle distance](./Middle_distance_track_event "Middle distance track event") runner and [world record holder](./World_record "World record") [Gunder Hägg](./Gunder_Hägg "Gunder Hägg"), who was born in the village [Albacken](./Albacken?action=edit&redlink=1 "Albacken") outside of the town Bräcke.

Debbie Kilroy

| Education | . [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland") |
| Occupations | [Human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist"), [prison reformer](./Prison_reform "Prison reform"), lawyer |
| Years active | 1992–present |
| Known for | Founder of [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside") |

**Debbie Kilroy** [OAM](./Medal_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Medal of the Order of Australia") (born 1961), née **Deborah Harding**, is an Australian [human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist") and [prison reformer](./Prison_reform "Prison reform"). She is known for having founded [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside"), an independent community organisation based in [Queensland](./Queensland "Queensland"), Australia, that advocates for the human rights of women and girls in the [criminal legal system](./Criminal_law "Criminal law"). She is a qualified lawyer, who in 2007 was the first person with serious convictions to be allowed to practise law by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland").

Early life and education
------------------------

Deborah[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Harding[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2) was born in 1961 in [Brisbane](./Brisbane "Brisbane"), and raised in the suburb of [Kedron](./Kedron,_Queensland "Kedron, Queensland"), Queensland. During her teens, she became rebellious, and, after being locked up at the age of 14 for a four-week psychiatric assessment, began a period of increasing criminalisation and imprisonment, with only brief periods out of the [criminal justice system](./Criminal_justice_system "Criminal justice system") during her teens. Witnessing and being a victim of injustices within the system, her early experiences with it made her angry.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

She had a child at the age of 18, and endured a [violent relationship](./Domestic_violence "Domestic violence") for some years. After leaving that relationship she met and in 1986 married her present husband, [rugby league](./Rugby_league "Rugby league") footballer [Joe Kilroy](./Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy"), and they had a child together. Debbie was sentenced to six years in prison[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) after having sold [cannabis](./Cannabis "Cannabis") to undercover police.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

In 1990, she witnessed her friend Debbie Dick being murdered in the overcrowded [Boggo Road Gaol](./Boggo_Road_Gaol "Boggo Road Gaol"),[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) and has said that "[her] commitment to fight against the criminalisation and imprisonment of women is in honour of her memory and the memories of all the women and girls who have died at the hands of the prison industrial complex". As a result of this murder, the prison authorities started involving prisoners in committees that helped to run the prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

During the three years that she served of her sentence before her release in 1992, she began training as a [social worker](./Social_worker "Social worker") through the [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"), determined to improve the situation of women and children in prison.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

Sisters Inside
--------------

Upon her release from prison in 1992, Kilroy started to establish Sisters Inside, an organisation dedicated to responding to the needs and human rights of criminalised women and the children affected by their imprisonment that were not being met by available services. At first Sisters Inside was a small group run mostly by volunteers, but it has grown into a larger community-based organisation providing a range of services to many women and children in Queensland.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) Author [Melissa Lucashenko](./Melissa_Lucashenko "Melissa Lucashenko") is a founding member.[[5]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-5)

The motto of Sisters Inside is "nothing about us without us".[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

Career
------

Kilroy completed her legal training as well as a Graduate Diploma in Forensic Mental Health (she is trained in [gestalt therapy](./Gestalt_therapy "Gestalt therapy")[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2)), and in 2017 was the first former prisoner to be admitted as a [legal practitioner](./Legal_practitioner "Legal practitioner") by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland"),[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) a decision ruled by Justice [Paul de Jersey](./Paul_de_Jersey "Paul de Jersey"), future [chief justice](./Chief_justice_of_Queensland "Chief justice of Queensland") and later [governor of Queensland](./Governor_of_Queensland "Governor of Queensland").[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

She opened her own legal practice in 2013.[[7]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-7)

Kilroy has served as an Executive Member of the [Queensland Council for Civil Liberties](./Queensland_Council_for_Civil_Liberties "Queensland Council for Civil Liberties") since 2001 and [ex-officio](./Ex-officio "Ex-officio") chairperson of the Youth Affairs Network of Queensland since 1997 (As of 2019[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit)). She has also served a member of a number of other bodies and organisations, including:[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

* the Criminal Law Committee;
* [Law Council of Australia](./Law_Council_of_Australia "Law Council of Australia")
* Criminal Law Committee, [Queensland Law Society](./Queensland_Law_Society "Queensland Law Society")
* Equal Rights Alliance
* Australian Women Again Violence Alliance
* National Coronial Reform, [Federation of Community Legal Centres](./Community_legal_centre "Community legal centre")
* Criminal Justice Network

She has been appointed to state and national working groups on a range of legal and social issues, and has also contributed to international forums, such as meetings convened by the [UN Office on Drugs and Crime](./UN_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime "UN Office on Drugs and Crime") to develop draft UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-Custodial Measures for Women Offenders; sessions of the Commission on the Status of Women; and conferences on [crime prevention](./Crime_prevention "Crime prevention") and criminal justice.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

In November 2016 Kilroy was appointed to Queensland's Sentencing Advisory Council.[[8]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-8) She believes that the council has an important role to play in educating the public, to counteract the "law-and-order hysteria" seen in the media and spruiked by politicians.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

In early 2019, she led a [crowd-funding](./Crowd-funding "Crowd-funding") campaign called #freeher to pay off the court debts of Indigenous women in [Western Australia](./Western_Australia "Western Australia") who had been imprisoned for defaulting on fines, raising over A$400,000 and enabling the release of 11 women.[[9]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-ausstory-9)[[10]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-10) Amendments to the WA legislation were passed in 2020, partly as result of the recommendation from the coronial inquiry into the [death of Ms Dhu](./Death_of_Ms_Dhu "Death of Ms Dhu"), who [died in police custody](./Aboriginal_deaths_in_custody "Aboriginal deaths in custody").[[11]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-11)

In April 2020 Kilroy contracted [COVID-19](./COVID-19 "COVID-19") after travelling to the United States with her friend and colleague Boneeta-Marie Mabo, with both becoming so unwell that they were admitted to hospital.[[12]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-12) Around 18 months of contracting the virus, in September 2021, she was still suffering from [Long COVID](./Long_COVID "Long COVID"), with a debilitating range of symptoms.[[13]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-13)

As of 2021[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit) she is principal of the law firm Kilroy & Callaghan, where she leads a team of five, and [CEO](./CEO "CEO") of Sisters Inside. She is passionate about encouraging former offenders, and in particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and [culturally diverse](./Multiculturalism_in_Australia#Terminology "Multiculturalism in Australia") women to become criminal lawyers.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

Beliefs and advocacy
--------------------

Kilroy's experience of imprisonment led to her belief that unnecessary trauma caused by the prison system, including [solitary confinement](./Solitary_confinement "Solitary confinement") as a punishment for [self-harm](./Self-harm "Self-harm"), leads to a greater likelihood of women re-offending and ending up back in prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Influenced by people such as the US academic, activist and former prisoner [Angela Davis](./Angela_Davis "Angela Davis"), Kilroy believes that the prison system fails in its mission to punish and rehabilitate, with more than half of women released from prison returning to spend another stint there.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She names two other former prisoners as heroes of hers: [Nelson Mandela](./Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](./Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi")[[14]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-14)

She has said that there is a need to break down "racism, misogyny and sexism within the legal frameworks", and that harsher sentences are not the answer.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She points out that "The vast majority of women prisoners are imprisoned for minor, non-violent crimes... [which] are often poverty-related", with around 40% being [onremand](./Remand_(detention) "Remand (detention)"), as yet untried for their alleged crimes. She says:[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

> Too often women are imprisoned on remand for failures of the state. Failure to provide adequate income support, to support women leaving violent homes, to provide essential housing and health services, and to address multigenerational harm arising from colonisation.

She engages in public debate and advocates for women on a range of issues, including violence, [homelessness](./Homelessness "Homelessness"), [racism](./Racism_in_Australia "Racism in Australia"), mental health, [substance abuse](./Substance_abuse "Substance abuse"), poverty, [child protection](./Child_protection "Child protection"), sexual assault, and failures in government systems. She aims to reduce the rate of criminalisation and imprisonment of women and children, in particular the over-representation of [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander](./Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander "Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander") within the criminal justice system, and to women reduce the impact of mothers' imprisonment on their children.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

Recognition
-----------

* 2003: [Order of Australia Medal](./Order_of_Australia_Medal "Order of Australia Medal")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2004: [Australian Human Rights Medal](./Australian_Human_Rights_Medal "Australian Human Rights Medal")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Emergent Woman Lawyer of the Year[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Peace Women Award[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2014: [Churchill Fellowship](./Churchill_Fellowship "Churchill Fellowship")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2016: shortlisted Queensland nomination for [Australian of the Year](./Australian_of_the_Year "Australian of the Year")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2019: keynote speaker at the [Law Institute of Victoria](./Law_Institute_of_Victoria "Law Institute of Victoria")'s Women in Leadership lunch[[15]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-15)
* 2019: [Voltaire Human Rights Award](./Voltaire_Human_Rights_Award "Voltaire Human Rights Award")[[16]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-16)

In media and the arts
---------------------

* *[Australian Story](./Australian_Story "Australian Story")* on [ABC Television](./ABC_Television_(Australia) "ABC Television (Australia)") (2004[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) and 2019)[[9]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-ausstory-9)
* *Kilroy was Here*, a biography by [Kristina Olsson](./Kristina_Olsson "Kristina Olsson") (2005)[[17]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-17)
* [Archibald Prize](./Archibald_Prize "Archibald Prize") entry (2005) and portrait by [Ai Wei Wei](./Ai_Wei_Wei "Ai Wei Wei") (2015)[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* *[The Drum](./The_Drum_(TV_program) "The Drum (TV program)")* on ABC Television[[18]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-drum2019-18)

Content:
Debbie Kilroy

Australian human rights activist and prison reformer

| Debbie Kilroy | |
| --- | --- |
| Born | Deborah Harding  1961 (age 64–65)  [Brisbane](./Brisbane "Brisbane"), [Queensland](./Queensland "Queensland"), Australia |
| Education | . [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland") |
| Occupations | [Human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist"), [prison reformer](./Prison_reform "Prison reform"), lawyer |
| Years active | 1992–present |
| Known for | Founder of [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside") |
| Spouse | [Joe Kilroy](./Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy") |
| Website | [www.sistersinside.com.au](https://www.sistersinside.com.au/) |

**Debbie Kilroy** [OAM](./Medal_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Medal of the Order of Australia") (born 1961), née **Deborah Harding**, is an Australian [human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist") and [prison reformer](./Prison_reform "Prison reform"). She is known for having founded [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside"), an independent community organisation based in [Queensland](./Queensland "Queensland"), Australia, that advocates for the human rights of women and girls in the [criminal legal system](./Criminal_law "Criminal law"). She is a qualified lawyer, who in 2007 was the first person with serious convictions to be allowed to practise law by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland").

Early life and education
------------------------

Deborah[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Harding[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2) was born in 1961 in [Brisbane](./Brisbane "Brisbane"), and raised in the suburb of [Kedron](./Kedron,_Queensland "Kedron, Queensland"), Queensland. During her teens, she became rebellious, and, after being locked up at the age of 14 for a four-week psychiatric assessment, began a period of increasing criminalisation and imprisonment, with only brief periods out of the [criminal justice system](./Criminal_justice_system "Criminal justice system") during her teens. Witnessing and being a victim of injustices within the system, her early experiences with it made her angry.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

She had a child at the age of 18, and endured a [violent relationship](./Domestic_violence "Domestic violence") for some years. After leaving that relationship she met and in 1986 married her present husband, [rugby league](./Rugby_league "Rugby league") footballer [Joe Kilroy](./Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy"), and they had a child together. Debbie was sentenced to six years in prison[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) after having sold [cannabis](./Cannabis "Cannabis") to undercover police.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

In 1990, she witnessed her friend Debbie Dick being murdered in the overcrowded [Boggo Road Gaol](./Boggo_Road_Gaol "Boggo Road Gaol"),[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) and has said that "[her] commitment to fight against the criminalisation and imprisonment of women is in honour of her memory and the memories of all the women and girls who have died at the hands of the prison industrial complex". As a result of this murder, the prison authorities started involving prisoners in committees that helped to run the prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

During the three years that she served of her sentence before her release in 1992, she began training as a [social worker](./Social_worker "Social worker") through the [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"), determined to improve the situation of women and children in prison.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

Sisters Inside
--------------

Upon her release from prison in 1992, Kilroy started to establish Sisters Inside, an organisation dedicated to responding to the needs and human rights of criminalised women and the children affected by their imprisonment that were not being met by available services. At first Sisters Inside was a small group run mostly by volunteers, but it has grown into a larger community-based organisation providing a range of services to many women and children in Queensland.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) Author [Melissa Lucashenko](./Melissa_Lucashenko "Melissa Lucashenko") is a founding member.[[5]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-5)

The motto of Sisters Inside is "nothing about us without us".[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

Career
------

Kilroy completed her legal training as well as a Graduate Diploma in Forensic Mental Health (she is trained in [gestalt therapy](./Gestalt_therapy "Gestalt therapy")[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2)), and in 2017 was the first former prisoner to be admitted as a [legal practitioner](./Legal_practitioner "Legal practitioner") by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland"),[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) a decision ruled by Justice [Paul de Jersey](./Paul_de_Jersey "Paul de Jersey"), future [chief justice](./Chief_justice_of_Queensland "Chief justice of Queensland") and later [governor of Queensland](./Governor_of_Queensland "Governor of Queensland").[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

She opened her own legal practice in 2013.[[7]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-7)

Kilroy has served as an Executive Member of the [Queensland Council for Civil Liberties](./Queensland_Council_for_Civil_Liberties "Queensland Council for Civil Liberties") since 2001 and [ex-officio](./Ex-officio "Ex-officio") chairperson of the Youth Affairs Network of Queensland since 1997 (As of 2019[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit)). She has also served a member of a number of other bodies and organisations, including:[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

* the Criminal Law Committee;
* [Law Council of Australia](./Law_Council_of_Australia "Law Council of Australia")
* Criminal Law Committee, [Queensland Law Society](./Queensland_Law_Society "Queensland Law Society")
* Equal Rights Alliance
* Australian Women Again Violence Alliance
* National Coronial Reform, [Federation of Community Legal Centres](./Community_legal_centre "Community legal centre")
* Criminal Justice Network

She has been appointed to state and national working groups on a range of legal and social issues, and has also contributed to international forums, such as meetings convened by the [UN Office on Drugs and Crime](./UN_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime "UN Office on Drugs and Crime") to develop draft UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-Custodial Measures for Women Offenders; sessions of the Commission on the Status of Women; and conferences on [crime prevention](./Crime_prevention "Crime prevention") and criminal justice.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

In November 2016 Kilroy was appointed to Queensland's Sentencing Advisory Council.[[8]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-8) She believes that the council has an important role to play in educating the public, to counteract the "law-and-order hysteria" seen in the media and spruiked by politicians.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

In early 2019, she led a [crowd-funding](./Crowd-funding "Crowd-funding") campaign called #freeher to pay off the court debts of Indigenous women in [Western Australia](./Western_Australia "Western Australia") who had been imprisoned for defaulting on fines, raising over A$400,000 and enabling the release of 11 women.[[9]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-ausstory-9)[[10]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-10) Amendments to the WA legislation were passed in 2020, partly as result of the recommendation from the coronial inquiry into the [death of Ms Dhu](./Death_of_Ms_Dhu "Death of Ms Dhu"), who [died in police custody](./Aboriginal_deaths_in_custody "Aboriginal deaths in custody").[[11]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-11)

In April 2020 Kilroy contracted [COVID-19](./COVID-19 "COVID-19") after travelling to the United States with her friend and colleague Boneeta-Marie Mabo, with both becoming so unwell that they were admitted to hospital.[[12]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-12) Around 18 months of contracting the virus, in September 2021, she was still suffering from [Long COVID](./Long_COVID "Long COVID"), with a debilitating range of symptoms.[[13]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-13)

As of 2021[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit) she is principal of the law firm Kilroy & Callaghan, where she leads a team of five, and [CEO](./CEO "CEO") of Sisters Inside. She is passionate about encouraging former offenders, and in particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and [culturally diverse](./Multiculturalism_in_Australia#Terminology "Multiculturalism in Australia") women to become criminal lawyers.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

Beliefs and advocacy
--------------------

Kilroy's experience of imprisonment led to her belief that unnecessary trauma caused by the prison system, including [solitary confinement](./Solitary_confinement "Solitary confinement") as a punishment for [self-harm](./Self-harm "Self-harm"), leads to a greater likelihood of women re-offending and ending up back in prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Influenced by people such as the US academic, activist and former prisoner [Angela Davis](./Angela_Davis "Angela Davis"), Kilroy believes that the prison system fails in its mission to punish and rehabilitate, with more than half of women released from prison returning to spend another stint there.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She names two other former prisoners as heroes of hers: [Nelson Mandela](./Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](./Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi")[[14]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-14)

She has said that there is a need to break down "racism, misogyny and sexism within the legal frameworks", and that harsher sentences are not the answer.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She points out that "The vast majority of women prisoners are imprisoned for minor, non-violent crimes... [which] are often poverty-related", with around 40% being [onremand](./Remand_(detention) "Remand (detention)"), as yet untried for their alleged crimes. She says:[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

> Too often women are imprisoned on remand for failures of the state. Failure to provide adequate income support, to support women leaving violent homes, to provide essential housing and health services, and to address multigenerational harm arising from colonisation.

She engages in public debate and advocates for women on a range of issues, including violence, [homelessness](./Homelessness "Homelessness"), [racism](./Racism_in_Australia "Racism in Australia"), mental health, [substance abuse](./Substance_abuse "Substance abuse"), poverty, [child protection](./Child_protection "Child protection"), sexual assault, and failures in government systems. She aims to reduce the rate of criminalisation and imprisonment of women and children, in particular the over-representation of [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander](./Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander "Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander") within the criminal justice system, and to women reduce the impact of mothers' imprisonment on their children.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

Recognition
-----------

* 2003: [Order of Australia Medal](./Order_of_Australia_Medal "Order of Australia Medal")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2004: [Australian Human Rights Medal](./Australian_Human_Rights_Medal "Australian Human Rights Medal")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Emergent Woman Lawyer of the Year[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Peace Women Award[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2014: [Churchill Fellowship](./Churchill_Fellowship "Churchill Fellowship")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2016: shortlisted Queensland nomination for [Australian of the Year](./Australian_of_the_Year "Australian of the Year")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2019: keynote speaker at the [Law Institute of Victoria](./Law_Institute_of_Victoria "Law Institute of Victoria")'s Women in Leadership lunch[[15]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-15)
* 2019: [Voltaire Human Rights Award](./Voltaire_Human_Rights_Award "Voltaire Human Rights Award")[[16]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-16)

In media and the arts
---------------------

* *[Australian Story](./Australian_Story "Australian Story")* on [ABC Television](./ABC_Television_(Australia) "ABC Television (Australia)") (2004[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) and 2019)[[9]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-ausstory-9)
* *Kilroy was Here*, a biography by [Kristina Olsson](./Kristina_Olsson "Kristina Olsson") (2005)[[17]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-17)
* [Archibald Prize](./Archibald_Prize "Archibald Prize") entry (2005) and portrait by [Ai Wei Wei](./Ai_Wei_Wei "Ai Wei Wei") (2015)[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* *[The Drum](./The_Drum_(TV_program) "The Drum (TV program)")* on ABC Television[[18]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-drum2019-18)

{"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "

You are a Web Agent, that is designed to manage and complete TASKs in iterative CYCLES based on input from the USER through Web protocols in the Web ENVIRONMENT.

TASK Definition
- A TASK is an instruction of the USER to achieve a specified purpose.
- A TASK requires multiple CYCLES to complete.
- Complete the TASK by only using the available TOOLS.

CYCLES Definition
- A CYCLE is specified through a Thought-Act-Observe pattern.
- 1) Thought: Carefully analyze the TASK and the descriptions in the representations gathered through the USER and previously observed information. Evaluate the completion status of the TASK.
- 2) Act: Formulate a plan with ACTIONS that directly contribute to completing the TASK, potentially across multiple CYCLES. Do NEVER expand beyond the original TASK boundaries.
- 3) Observe: The USER and the ENVIRONMENT can provide observations that help to refine the plan.

LOOP Definition
- A LOOP is a sequence of CYCLES that is used to finish a TASK.
- Once the LOOP is finished you MUST call `final_answer` to report the result.

TOOLS
- A TOOL is an operation that allows you to percieve or interact with the ENVIRONMENT.
- During each CYCLE, invoke one or multiple TOOLS.
- The following TOOLS are available to you:

- **get**: Fetches a URL and returns the resource content. Takes a URL as input and returns the the URL with the resource content.
  - Inputs:
  
    - `url` (string): The URL to fetch and the resource content.
  
  - Output: string

**Bräcke Municipality** ([Swedish](./Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Bräcke kommun*) is a [municipality](./Municipalities_of_Sweden "Municipalities of Sweden") in [Jämtland County](./Jämtland_County "Jämtland County") in northern [Sweden](./Sweden "Sweden"). Its [seat](./Administrative_centre "Administrative centre") is located in [Bräcke](./Bräcke "Bräcke").

The present municipality was formed in 1974 when "old" Bräcke Municipality was amalgamated with Kälarne and Revsund. The three former municipalities had been created in 1952. The number of original entities (as of 1863) were six. Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.

**Debbie Kilroy** [OAM](./Medal_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Medal of the Order of Australia") (born 1961), née **Deborah Harding**, is an Australian [human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist") and [prison reformer](./Prison_reform "Prison reform"). She is known for having founded [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside"), an independent community organisation based in [Queensland](./Queensland "Queensland"), Australia, that advocates for the human rights of women and girls in the [criminal legal system](./Criminal_law "Criminal law"). She is a qualified lawyer, who in 2007 was the first person with serious convictions to be allowed to practise law by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland").

Early life and education
------------------------

Deborah[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Harding[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2) was born in 1961 in [Brisbane](./Brisbane "Brisbane"), and raised in the suburb of [Kedron](./Kedron,_Queensland "Kedron, Queensland"), Queensland. During her teens, she became rebellious, and, after being locked up at the age of 14 for a four-week psychiatric assessment, began a period of increasing criminalisation and imprisonment, with only brief periods out of the [criminal justice system](./Criminal_justice_system "Criminal justice system") during her teens. Witnessing and being a victim of injustices within the system, her early experiences with it made her angry.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

She had a child at the age of 18, and endured a [violent relationship](./Domestic_violence "Domestic violence") for some years. After leaving that relationship she met and in 1986 married her present husband, [rugby league](./Rugby_league "Rugby league") footballer [Joe Kilroy](./Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy"), and they had a child together. Debbie was sentenced to six years in prison[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) after having sold [cannabis](./Cannabis "Cannabis") to undercover police.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

In 1990, she witnessed her friend Debbie Dick being murdered in the overcrowded [Boggo Road Gaol](./Boggo_Road_Gaol "Boggo Road Gaol"),[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) and has said that "[her] commitment to fight against the criminalisation and imprisonment of women is in honour of her memory and the memories of all the women and girls who have died at the hands of the prison industrial complex". As a result of this murder, the prison authorities started involving prisoners in committees that helped to run the prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

During the three years that she served of her sentence before her release in 1992, she began training as a [social worker](./Social_worker "Social worker") through the [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"), determined to improve the situation of women and children in prison.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

Sisters Inside
--------------

Upon her release from prison in 1992, Kilroy started to establish Sisters Inside, an organisation dedicated to responding to the needs and human rights of criminalised women and the children affected by their imprisonment that were not being met by available services. At first Sisters Inside was a small group run mostly by volunteers, but it has grown into a larger community-based organisation providing a range of services to many women and children in Queensland.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) Author [Melissa Lucashenko](./Melissa_Lucashenko "Melissa Lucashenko") is a founding member.[[5]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-5)

The motto of Sisters Inside is "nothing about us without us".[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

Career
------

Kilroy completed her legal training as well as a Graduate Diploma in Forensic Mental Health (she is trained in [gestalt therapy](./Gestalt_therapy "Gestalt therapy")[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2)), and in 2017 was the first former prisoner to be admitted as a [legal practitioner](./Legal_practitioner "Legal practitioner") by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland"),[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) a decision ruled by Justice [Paul de Jersey](./Paul_de_Jersey "Paul de Jersey"), future [chief justice](./Chief_justice_of_Queensland "Chief justice of Queensland") and later [governor of Queensland](./Governor_of_Queensland "Governor of Queensland").[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

She opened her own legal practice in 2013.[[7]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-7)

Kilroy has served as an Executive Member of the [Queensland Council for Civil Liberties](./Queensland_Council_for_Civil_Liberties "Queensland Council for Civil Liberties") since 2001 and [ex-officio](./Ex-officio "Ex-officio") chairperson of the Youth Affairs Network of Queensland since 1997 (As of 2019[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit)). She has also served a member of a number of other bodies and organisations, including:[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

* the Criminal Law Committee;
* [Law Council of Australia](./Law_Council_of_Australia "Law Council of Australia")
* Criminal Law Committee, [Queensland Law Society](./Queensland_Law_Society "Queensland Law Society")
* Equal Rights Alliance
* Australian Women Again Violence Alliance
* National Coronial Reform, [Federation of Community Legal Centres](./Community_legal_centre "Community legal centre")
* Criminal Justice Network

She has been appointed to state and national working groups on a range of legal and social issues, and has also contributed to international forums, such as meetings convened by the [UN Office on Drugs and Crime](./UN_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime "UN Office on Drugs and Crime") to develop draft UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-Custodial Measures for Women Offenders; sessions of the Commission on the Status of Women; and conferences on [crime prevention](./Crime_prevention "Crime prevention") and criminal justice.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

In November 2016 Kilroy was appointed to Queensland's Sentencing Advisory Council.[[8]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-8) She believes that the council has an important role to play in educating the public, to counteract the "law-and-order hysteria" seen in the media and spruiked by politicians.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

In early 2019, she led a [crowd-funding](./Crowd-funding "Crowd-funding") campaign called #freeher to pay off the court debts of Indigenous women in [Western Australia](./Western_Australia "Western Australia") who had been imprisoned for defaulting on fines, raising over A$400,000 and enabling the release of 11 women.[[9]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-ausstory-9)[[10]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-10) Amendments to the WA legislation were passed in 2020, partly as result of the recommendation from the coronial inquiry into the [death of Ms Dhu](./Death_of_Ms_Dhu "Death of Ms Dhu"), who [died in police custody](./Aboriginal_deaths_in_custody "Aboriginal deaths in custody").[[11]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-11)

In April 2020 Kilroy contracted [COVID-19](./COVID-19 "COVID-19") after travelling to the United States with her friend and colleague Boneeta-Marie Mabo, with both becoming so unwell that they were admitted to hospital.[[12]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-12) Around 18 months of contracting the virus, in September 2021, she was still suffering from [Long COVID](./Long_COVID "Long COVID"), with a debilitating range of symptoms.[[13]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-13)

As of 2021[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit) she is principal of the law firm Kilroy & Callaghan, where she leads a team of five, and [CEO](./CEO "CEO") of Sisters Inside. She is passionate about encouraging former offenders, and in particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and [culturally diverse](./Multiculturalism_in_Australia#Terminology "Multiculturalism in Australia") women to become criminal lawyers.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

Beliefs and advocacy
--------------------

Kilroy's experience of imprisonment led to her belief that unnecessary trauma caused by the prison system, including [solitary confinement](./Solitary_confinement "Solitary confinement") as a punishment for [self-harm](./Self-harm "Self-harm"), leads to a greater likelihood of women re-offending and ending up back in prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Influenced by people such as the US academic, activist and former prisoner [Angela Davis](./Angela_Davis "Angela Davis"), Kilroy believes that the prison system fails in its mission to punish and rehabilitate, with more than half of women released from prison returning to spend another stint there.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She names two other former prisoners as heroes of hers: [Nelson Mandela](./Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](./Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi")[[14]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-14)

She has said that there is a need to break down "racism, misogyny and sexism within the legal frameworks", and that harsher sentences are not the answer.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She points out that "The vast majority of women prisoners are imprisoned for minor, non-violent crimes... [which] are often poverty-related", with around 40% being [onremand](./Remand_(detention) "Remand (detention)"), as yet untried for their alleged crimes. She says:[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

> Too often women are imprisoned on remand for failures of the state. Failure to provide adequate income support, to support women leaving violent homes, to provide essential housing and health services, and to address multigenerational harm arising from colonisation.

She engages in public debate and advocates for women on a range of issues, including violence, [homelessness](./Homelessness "Homelessness"), [racism](./Racism_in_Australia "Racism in Australia"), mental health, [substance abuse](./Substance_abuse "Substance abuse"), poverty, [child protection](./Child_protection "Child protection"), sexual assault, and failures in government systems. She aims to reduce the rate of criminalisation and imprisonment of women and children, in particular the over-representation of [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander](./Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander "Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander") within the criminal justice system, and to women reduce the impact of mothers' imprisonment on their children.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

Recognition
-----------

* 2003: [Order of Australia Medal](./Order_of_Australia_Medal "Order of Australia Medal")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2004: [Australian Human Rights Medal](./Australian_Human_Rights_Medal "Australian Human Rights Medal")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Emergent Woman Lawyer of the Year[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Peace Women Award[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2014: [Churchill Fellowship](./Churchill_Fellowship "Churchill Fellowship")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2016: shortlisted Queensland nomination for [Australian of the Year](./Australian_of_the_Year "Australian of the Year")[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2019: keynote speaker at the [Law Institute of Victoria](./Law_Institute_of_Victoria "Law Institute of Victoria")'s Women in Leadership lunch[[15]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-15)
* 2019: [Voltaire Human Rights Award](./Voltaire_Human_Rights_Award "Voltaire Human Rights Award")[[16]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-16)

**Bräcke Municipality** ([Swedish](./Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Bräcke kommun*) is a [municipality](./Municipalities_of_Sweden "Municipalities of Sweden") in [Jämtland County](./Jämtland_County "Jämtland County") in northern [Sweden](./Sweden "Sweden"). Its [seat](./Administrative_centre "Administrative centre") is located in [Bräcke](./Bräcke "Bräcke").

The present municipality was formed in 1974 when "old" Bräcke Municipality was amalgamated with Kälarne and Revsund. The three former municipalities had been created in 1952. The number of original entities (as of 1863) were six. Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.

One of the most famous people coming from Bräcke Municipality is the former [middle distance](./Middle_distance_track_event "Middle distance track event") runner and [world record holder](./World_record "World record") [Gunder Hägg](./Gunder_Hägg "Gunder Hägg"), who was born in the village [Albacken](./Albacken?action=edit&redlink=1 "Albacken") outside of the town Bräcke.

Debbie Kilroy

Australian human rights activist and prison reformer

**Debbie Kilroy** [OAM](./Medal_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Medal of the Order of Australia") (born 1961), née **Deborah Harding**, is an Australian [human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist") and [prison reformer](./Prison_reform "Prison reform"). She is known for having founded [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside"), an independent community organisation based in [Queensland](./Queensland "Queensland"), Australia, that advocates for the human rights of women and girls in the [criminal legal system](./Criminal_law "Criminal law"). She is a qualified lawyer, who in 2007 was the first person with serious convictions to be allowed to practise law by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland").

Early life and education
------------------------

Deborah[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Harding[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2) was born in 1961 in [Brisbane](./Brisbane "Brisbane"), and raised in the suburb of [Kedron](./Kedron,_Queensland "Kedron, Queensland"), Queensland. During her teens, she became rebellious, and, after being locked up at the age of 14 for a four-week psychiatric assessment, began a period of increasing criminalisation and imprisonment, with only brief periods out of the [criminal justice system](./Criminal_justice_system "Criminal justice system") during her teens. Witnessing and being a victim of injustices within the system, her early experiences with it made her angry.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

She had a child at the age of 18, and endured a [violent relationship](./Domestic_violence "Domestic violence") for some years. After leaving that relationship she met and in 1986 married her present husband, [rugby league](./Rugby_league "Rugby league") footballer [Joe Kilroy](./Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy"), and they had a child together. Debbie was sentenced to six years in prison[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) after having sold [cannabis](./Cannabis "Cannabis") to undercover police.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

In 1990, she witnessed her friend Debbie Dick being murdered in the overcrowded [Boggo Road Gaol](./Boggo_Road_Gaol "Boggo Road Gaol"),[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) and has said that "[her] commitment to fight against the criminalisation and imprisonment of women is in honour of her memory and the memories of all the women and girls who have died at the hands of the prison industrial complex". As a result of this murder, the prison authorities started involving prisoners in committees that helped to run the prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

During the three years that she served of her sentence before her release in 1992, she began training as a [social worker](./Social_worker "Social worker") through the [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"), determined to improve the situation of women and children in prison.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

Sisters Inside
--------------

Upon her release from prison in 1992, Kilroy started to establish Sisters Inside, an organisation dedicated to responding to the needs and human rights of criminalised women and the children affected by their imprisonment that were not being met by available services. At first Sisters Inside was a small group run mostly by volunteers, but it has grown into a larger community-based organisation providing a range of services to many women and children in Queensland.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) Author [Melissa Lucashenko](./Melissa_Lucashenko "Melissa Lucashenko") is a founding member.[[5]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-5)

The motto of Sisters Inside is "nothing about us without us".[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

Career
------

Kilroy completed her legal training as well as a Graduate Diploma in Forensic Mental Health (she is trained in [gestalt therapy](./Gestalt_therapy "Gestalt therapy")[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2)), and in 2017 was the first former prisoner to be admitted as a [legal practitioner](./Legal_practitioner "Legal practitioner") by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland"),[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) a decision ruled by Justice [Paul de Jersey](./Paul_de_Jersey "Paul de Jersey"), future [chief justice](./Chief_justice_of_Queensland "Chief justice of Queensland") and later [governor of Queensland](./Governor_of_Queensland "Governor of Queensland").[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

She opened her own legal practice in 2013.[[7]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-7)

Kilroy has served as an Executive Member of the [Queensland Council for Civil Liberties](./Queensland_Council_for_Civil_Liberties "Queensland Council for Civil Liberties") since 2001 and [ex-officio](./Ex-officio "Ex-officio") chairperson of the Youth Affairs Network of Queensland since 1997 (As of 2019[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit)). She has also served a member of a number of other bodies and organisations, including:[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

* the Criminal Law Committee;
* [Law Council of Australia](./Law_Council_of_Australia "Law Council of Australia")
* Criminal Law Committee, [Queensland Law Society](./Queensland_Law_Society "Queensland Law Society")
* Equal Rights Alliance
* Australian Women Again Violence Alliance
* National Coronial Reform, [Federation of Community Legal Centres](./Community_legal_centre "Community legal centre")
* Criminal Justice Network

She has been appointed to state and national working groups on a range of legal and social issues, and has also contributed to international forums, such as meetings convened by the [UN Office on Drugs and Crime](./UN_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime "UN Office on Drugs and Crime") to develop draft UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-Custodial Measures for Women Offenders; sessions of the Commission on the Status of Women; and conferences on [crime prevention](./Crime_prevention "Crime prevention") and criminal justice.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

In November 2016 Kilroy was appointed to Queensland's Sentencing Advisory Council.[[8]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-8) She believes that the council has an important role to play in educating the public, to counteract the "law-and-order hysteria" seen in the media and spruiked by politicians.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

In early 2019, she led a [crowd-funding](./Crowd-funding "Crowd-funding") campaign called #freeher to pay off the court debts of Indigenous women in [Western Australia](./Western_Australia "Western Australia") who had been imprisoned for defaulting on fines, raising over A$400,000 and enabling the release of 11 women.[[9]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-ausstory-9)[[10]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-10) Amendments to the WA legislation were passed in 2020, partly as result of the recommendation from the coronial inquiry into the [death of Ms Dhu](./Death_of_Ms_Dhu "Death of Ms Dhu"), who [died in police custody](./Aboriginal_deaths_in_custody "Aboriginal deaths in custody").[[11]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-11)

In April 2020 Kilroy contracted [COVID-19](./COVID-19 "COVID-19") after travelling to the United States with her friend and colleague Boneeta-Marie Mabo, with both becoming so unwell that they were admitted to hospital.[[12]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-12) Around 18 months of contracting the virus, in September 2021, she was still suffering from [Long COVID](./Long_COVID "Long COVID"), with a debilitating range of symptoms.[[13]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-13)

As of 2021[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit) she is principal of the law firm Kilroy & Callaghan, where she leads a team of five, and [CEO](./CEO "CEO") of Sisters Inside. She is passionate about encouraging former offenders, and in particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and [culturally diverse](./Multiculturalism_in_Australia#Terminology "Multiculturalism in Australia") women to become criminal lawyers.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)

Beliefs and advocacy
--------------------

Kilroy's experience of imprisonment led to her belief that unnecessary trauma caused by the prison system, including [solitary confinement](./Solitary_confinement "Solitary confinement") as a punishment for [self-harm](./Self-harm "Self-harm"), leads to a greater likelihood of women re-offending and ending up back in prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Influenced by people such as the US academic, activist and former prisoner [Angela Davis](./Angela_Davis "Angela Davis"), Kilroy believes that the prison system fails in its mission to punish and rehabilitate, with more than half of women released from prison returning to spend another stint there.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She names two other former prisoners as heroes of hers: [Nelson Mandela](./Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](./Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi")[[14]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-14)

She has said that there is a need to break down "racism, misogyny and sexism within the legal frameworks", and that harsher sentences are not the answer.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She points out that "The vast majority of women prisoners are imprisoned for minor, non-violent crimes... [which] are often poverty-related", with around 40% being [onremand](./Remand_(detention) "Remand (detention)"), as yet untried for their alleged crimes. She says:[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)

> Too often women are imprisoned on remand for failures of the state. Failure to provide adequate income support, to support women leaving violent homes, to provide essential housing and health services, and to address multigenerational harm arising from colonisation.

She engages in public debate and advocates for women on a range of issues, including violence, [homelessness](./Homelessness "Homelessness"), [racism](./Racism_in_Australia "Racism in Australia"), mental health, [substance abuse](./Substance_abuse "Substance abuse"), poverty, [child protection](./Child_protection "Child protection"), sexual assault, and failures in government systems. She aims to reduce the rate of criminalisation and imprisonment of women and children, in particular the over-representation of [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander](./Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander "Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander") within the criminal justice system, and to women reduce the impact of mothers' imprisonment on their children.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)

-----------

Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.\\n\\nLocalities\\n----------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Br%C3%A4ckeCity.jpg/250px-Br%C3%A4ckeCity.jpg)](./File:BräckeCity.jpg)\\n\\nCentral [Bräcke](./Bräcke \"Bräcke\").\\n\\nThere are four [localities](./Urban_areas_in_Sweden \"Urban areas in Sweden\") (or urban areas) in Bräcke Municipality:[[3]](./Bräcke_Municipality#cite_note-3)\\n\\n| # | Locality | Population |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| 1 | **[Bräcke](./Bräcke \"Bräcke\")** | 1,566 |\\n| 2 | [Gällö](./Gällö \"Gällö\") | 758 |\\n| 3 | [Kälarne](./Kälarne \"Kälarne\") | 492 |\\n| 4 | [Pilgrimstad](./Pilgrimstad \"Pilgrimstad\") | 405 |\\n\\nThe municipal seat in [bold](./Emphasis_(typography) \"Emphasis (typography)\")\\n\\nDemographics\\n------------\\n\\nThis is a demographic table based on Bräcke Municipality\\'s electoral districts in the [2022 Swedish general election](./2022_Swedish_general_election \"2022 Swedish general election\") sourced from [SVT](./Swedish_Television \"Swedish Television\")\\'s election platform, in turn taken from [SCB](./Statistiska_Centralbyrån \"Statistiska Centralbyrån\") official statistics.[[4]](./Bräcke_Municipality#cite_note-BräckeVal2022-4)\\n\\nIn total there were 6,167 residents, including 4,820 Swedish citizens of voting age.[[4]](./Bräcke_Municipality#cite_note-BräckeVal2022-4) 52.1% voted for the left coalition and 46.7% for the right coalition. content=[{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Observation:\\nURL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Kilroy\\n\\nStatus Code: 200\\n\\nContent:\\nDebbie Kilroy\\n\\nAustralian human rights activist and prison reformer\\n\\n| Debbie Kilroy | |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Born | Deborah Harding  1961 (age\\xa064–65)  [Brisbane](./Brisbane \"Brisbane\"), [Queensland](./Queensland \"Queensland\"), Australia |\\n| Education | . [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland \"University of Queensland\") |\\n| Occupations | [Human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist \"Human rights activist\"), [prison reformer](./Prison_reform \"Prison reform\"), lawyer |\\n| Years\\xa0active | 1992–present |\\n| Known\\xa0for | Founder of [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside \"Sisters Inside\") |\\n| Spouse | [Joe Kilroy](./Joe_Kilroy \"Joe Kilroy\") |\\n| Website | [www.sistersinside.com.au](https://www.sistersinside.com.au/) |\\n\\n**Debbie Kilroy** [OAM](./Medal_of_the_Order_of_Australia \"Medal of the Order of Australia\") (born 1961), née **Deborah Harding**, is an Australian [human rights activist](./Human_rights_activist \"Human rights activist\") and [prison reformer](./Prison_reform \"Prison reform\"). She is known for having founded [Sisters Inside](./Sisters_Inside \"Sisters Inside\"), an independent community organisation based in [Queensland](./Queensland \"Queensland\"), Australia, that advocates for the human rights of women and girls in the [criminal legal system](./Criminal_law \"Criminal law\"). She is a qualified lawyer, who in 2007 was the first person with serious convictions to be allowed to practise law by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland \"Supreme Court of Queensland\").\\n\\nEarly life and education\\n------------------------\\n\\nDeborah[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Harding[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2) was born in 1961 in [Brisbane](./Brisbane \"Brisbane\"), and raised in the suburb of [Kedron](./Kedron,_Queensland \"Kedron, Queensland\"), Queensland. During her teens, she became rebellious, and, after being locked up at the age of 14 for a four-week psychiatric assessment, began a period of increasing criminalisation and imprisonment, with only brief periods out of the [criminal justice system](./Criminal_justice_system \"Criminal justice system\") during her teens. Witnessing and being a victim of injustices within the system, her early experiences with it made her angry.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)\\n\\nShe had a child at the age of 18, and endured a [violent relationship](./Domestic_violence \"Domestic violence\") for some years. After leaving that relationship she met and in 1986 married her present husband, [rugby league](./Rugby_league \"Rugby league\") footballer [Joe Kilroy](./Joe_Kilroy \"Joe Kilroy\"), and they had a child together. Debbie was sentenced to six years in prison[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) after having sold [cannabis](./Cannabis \"Cannabis\") to undercover police.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)\\n\\nIn 1990, she witnessed her friend Debbie Dick being murdered in the overcrowded [Boggo Road Gaol](./Boggo_Road_Gaol \"Boggo Road Gaol\"),[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) and has said that \"[her] commitment to fight against the criminalisation and imprisonment of women is in honour of her memory and the memories of all the women and girls who have died at the hands of the prison industrial complex\". As a result of this murder, the prison authorities started involving prisoners in committees that helped to run the prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)\\n\\nDuring the three years that she served of her sentence before her release in 1992, she began training as a [social worker](./Social_worker \"Social worker\") through the [University of Queensland](./University_of_Queensland \"University of Queensland\"), determined to improve the situation of women and children in prison.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)\\n\\nSisters Inside\\n--------------\\n\\nUpon her release from prison in 1992, Kilroy started to establish Sisters Inside, an organisation dedicated to responding to the needs and human rights of criminalised women and the children affected by their imprisonment that were not being met by available services. At first Sisters Inside was a small group run mostly by volunteers, but it has grown into a larger community-based organisation providing a range of services to many women and children in Queensland.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) Author [Melissa Lucashenko](./Melissa_Lucashenko \"Melissa Lucashenko\") is a founding member.[[5]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-5)\\n\\nThe motto of Sisters Inside is \"nothing about us without us\".[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)\\n\\nCareer\\n------\\n\\nKilroy completed her legal training as well as a Graduate Diploma in Forensic Mental Health (she is trained in [gestalt therapy](./Gestalt_therapy \"Gestalt therapy\")[[2]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-wmoa-2)), and in 2017 was the first former prisoner to be admitted as a [legal practitioner](./Legal_practitioner \"Legal practitioner\") by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](./Supreme_Court_of_Queensland \"Supreme Court of Queensland\"),[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3) a decision ruled by Justice [Paul de Jersey](./Paul_de_Jersey \"Paul de Jersey\"), future [chief justice](./Chief_justice_of_Queensland \"Chief justice of Queensland\") and later [governor of Queensland](./Governor_of_Queensland \"Governor of Queensland\").[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)\\n\\nShe opened her own legal practice in 2013.[[7]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-7)\\n\\nKilroy has served as an Executive Member of the [Queensland Council for Civil Liberties](./Queensland_Council_for_Civil_Liberties \"Queensland Council for Civil Liberties\") since 2001 and [ex-officio](./Ex-officio \"Ex-officio\") chairperson of the Youth Affairs Network of Queensland since 1997 (As of 2019[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit)). She has also served a member of a number of other bodies and organisations, including:[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)\\n\\n* the Criminal Law Committee;\\n* [Law Council of Australia](./Law_Council_of_Australia \"Law Council of Australia\")\\n* Criminal Law Committee, [Queensland Law Society](./Queensland_Law_Society \"Queensland Law Society\")\\n* Equal Rights Alliance\\n* Australian Women Again Violence Alliance\\n* National Coronial Reform, [Federation of Community Legal Centres](./Community_legal_centre \"Community legal centre\")\\n* Criminal Justice Network\\n\\nShe has been appointed to state and national working groups on a range of legal and social issues, and has also contributed to international forums, such as meetings convened by the [UN Office on Drugs and Crime](./UN_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime \"UN Office on Drugs and Crime\") to develop draft UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-Custodial Measures for Women Offenders; sessions of the Commission on the Status of Women; and conferences on [crime prevention](./Crime_prevention \"Crime prevention\") and criminal justice.[[3]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-womensreg-3)\\n\\nIn November 2016 Kilroy was appointed to Queensland\\'s Sentencing Advisory Council.[[8]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-8) She believes that the council has an important role to play in educating the public, to counteract the \"law-and-order hysteria\" seen in the media and spruiked by politicians.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4)\\n\\nIn early 2019, she led a [crowd-funding](./Crowd-funding \"Crowd-funding\") campaign called #freeher to pay off the court debts of Indigenous women in [Western Australia](./Western_Australia \"Western Australia\") who had been imprisoned for defaulting on fines, raising over A$400,000 and enabling the release of 11 women.[[9]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-ausstory-9)[[10]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-10) Amendments to the WA legislation were passed in 2020, partly as result of the recommendation from the coronial inquiry into the [death of Ms Dhu](./Death_of_Ms_Dhu \"Death of Ms Dhu\"), who [died in police custody](./Aboriginal_deaths_in_custody \"Aboriginal deaths in custody\").[[11]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-11)\\n\\nIn April 2020 Kilroy contracted [COVID-19](./COVID-19 \"COVID-19\") after travelling to the United States with her friend and colleague Boneeta-Marie Mabo, with both becoming so unwell that they were admitted to hospital.[[12]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-12) Around 18 months of contracting the virus, in September 2021, she was still suffering from [Long COVID](./Long_COVID \"Long COVID\"), with a debilitating range of symptoms.[[13]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-13)\\n\\nAs of 2021[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit) she is principal of the law firm Kilroy & Callaghan, where she leads a team of five, and [CEO](./CEO \"CEO\") of Sisters Inside. She is passionate about encouraging former offenders, and in particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and [culturally diverse](./Multiculturalism_in_Australia#Terminology \"Multiculturalism in Australia\") women to become criminal lawyers.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1)\\n\\nBeliefs and advocacy\\n--------------------\\n\\nKilroy\\'s experience of imprisonment led to her belief that unnecessary trauma caused by the prison system, including [solitary confinement](./Solitary_confinement \"Solitary confinement\") as a punishment for [self-harm](./Self-harm \"Self-harm\"), leads to a greater likelihood of women re-offending and ending up back in prison.[[1]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-costi-1) Influenced by people such as the US academic, activist and former prisoner [Angela Davis](./Angela_Davis \"Angela Davis\"), Kilroy believes that the prison system fails in its mission to punish and rehabilitate, with more than half of women released from prison returning to spend another stint there.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She names two other former prisoners as heroes of hers: [Nelson Mandela](./Nelson_Mandela \"Nelson Mandela\") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](./Aung_San_Suu_Kyi \"Aung San Suu Kyi\")[[14]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-14)\\n\\nShe has said that there is a need to break down \"racism, misogyny and sexism within the legal frameworks\", and that harsher sentences are not the answer.[[4]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She points out that \"The vast majority of women prisoners are imprisoned for minor, non-violent crimes... [which] are often poverty-related\", with around 40% being [onremand](./Remand_(detention) \"Remand (detention)\"), as yet untried for their alleged crimes. She says:[[6]](./Debbie_Kilroy#cite_note-shedefined-6)\\n\\n> Too often women are imprisoned on remand for failures of the state. Failure to provide adequate income support, to support women leaving violent homes, to provide essential housing and health services, and to address multigenerational harm arising from colonisation.\\n\\nShe engages in public debate and advocates for women on a range of issues, including violence, [homelessness](./Homelessness \"Homelessness\"), [racism](./Racism_in_Australia \"Racism in Australia\"), mental health, [substance abuse](./Substance_abuse \"Substance abuse\"), poverty, [child protection](./Child_protection \"Child protection\"), sexual assault, and failures in government systems. She aims to reduce the rate of criminalisation and imprisonment of women and children, in particular the over-representation of [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander](./Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander \"Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander\") within the criminal justice system, and to women reduce the impact of mothers\\' imprisonment on their
